title: Greetings and names
goal: Greet people, give your name and say where you come from — while discovering Swedish's biggest gift: its verbs never change according to who is doing the action.
bekal: say hello and goodbye with the words Swedes actually use
give your name with *jag heter* and your origin with *jag kommer från*
use eight personal pronouns with one and the same verb form

dialogs.title: Dialogue — I korridoren
dialogs.intro: Dian's first day at the Lappis student housing in Stockholm. She is dragging her suitcase down the corridor when someone steps out of the kitchen with a cup of coffee.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ja, jag är ny. Jag heter Dian.
lines.id: Yes, I'm new. My name's Dian.
lines.literal: yes, I am new. I am-called Dian.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Trevligt! Jag heter Elin. Jag bor i rum tolv.
lines.id: Nice to meet you! I'm Elin. I live in room twelve.
lines.literal: pleasant! I am-called Elin. I live in room twelve.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Trevligt att träffas. Var kommer du ifrån?
lines.id: Nice to meet you. Where are you from?
lines.literal: pleasant to meet. where come you from?

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Jag är svensk. Jag kommer från Göteborg. Och du?
lines.id: I'm Swedish. I'm from Gothenburg. And you?
lines.literal: I am Swedish. I come from Göteborg. and you?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag kommer från Indonesien. Jag är student här.
lines.id: I'm from Indonesia. I'm a student here.
lines.literal: I come from Indonesia. I am student here.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.id: How fun! Do you speak Swedish?

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Bra! Då pratar vi svenska, va?
lines.id: Great! Then we'll speak Swedish, OK?
lines.literal: good! then talk we Swedish, eh?

notes: **Hej** is the greeting for anyone, at any time — friends, teachers, cashiers, government ministers. Swedish hardly uses time-of-day greetings at all. *God morgon* does exist, but it sounds formal; *god dag* is almost only heard in old films. When in doubt, say *hej* — and if you want to sound warmer, say it twice: **hej hej**.

**Jag heter Dian** literally means "I am called Dian". Swedish introduces people with the verb *att heta* (to be called) rather than "my name is…". *Mitt namn är Dian* is correct, but it sounds like you're filling in an immigration form. Use *jag heter*.

**Here is the big gift.** Look at *jag är* and *är du* — exactly the same verb form. The same goes for *jag heter* / *du heter*, *jag bor* / *bor du*, *jag kommer* / *kommer du*. Swedish verbs **do not change at all** according to who is doing the action. No *am/is/are*, no *-s* for he/she/it. One form for all eight persons — after English, that's a real relief.

**Jag is pronounced "yah"**, not "yag". The *g* at the end of *jag* and *dag* is usually silent in speech. And **är is pronounced "eh"** — the *r* almost disappears. So *jag är* comes out as **yah eh**, two short sounds glued into one. It's the most frequent word pair in the whole language, so get the sound right now.

**Trevligt** is pronounced **TREV-lit** — the *g* in the ending *-igt* is silent. The word is used for people, evenings, conversations, restaurants: anything that feels pleasant. *Trevligt att träffas* is the standard phrase when you meet someone, and you'll hear it hundreds of times.

**Vi ses** literally means "we see each other" — a reciprocal form made with an *-s* ending. Together with *hej då*, it's the most common way friends say goodbye. Verbs with this reciprocal *-s* are covered properly at A2; for now, learn *vi ses* and *vi hörs* as whole phrases.

grammars.title: One verb form for everyone
body: This table is the reason Swedish feels light in the first week. Read each column from top to bottom: nothing changes.
after: Compare English (*I am, you are, he is*) or French (*je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes*). Swedish has thrown all of that away. All you need to learn is **one form per verb**.

The pronoun **de** (they) is pronounced **dom**, and so is *dem* (them). Don't try to pronounce the letters as written — no Swede says "de" the way it's spelled. In text messages, many Swedes simply write *dom*.

**Ni** means "you" when you're talking to more than one person. It used to be the polite "you" for one person as well, but since the *du-reformen* of the 1960s, Swedes say **du** to everyone — teachers, doctors, bosses, even the prime minister. Using *ni* to a single older person can actually sound odd rather than polite.

sections.title: Saying where you're from, your nationality and your language

blocks.text: Several patterns are used interchangeably, and they're all equally correct:

Notice there's **no article** in front of languages and nationalities: not *jag talar den svenska*, just *jag talar svenska* — exactly as in English. But unlike English, languages and nationalities are written with a **small letter**: *svenska*, *engelska*, *indonesiska*. Country names keep their capital: *Sverige*, *Indonesien*.

**Kina** is pronounced **SHEE-nah**, not "keena": a *k* in front of *i* turns into a soft hissing *sh*. The same rule turns *köpa* into **SHÖ-pah** and *kyrka* into **SHÜR-kah**. It applies before *e, i, y, ä, ö* — those five vowels only.

sections.title: Why this feels easy for an English speaker

blocks.text: The first unit of most language courses walks you straight into a wall. There's no wall here, and that's no accident — Swedish and English are close relatives, and three features make the start especially gentle:

items: **Verbs don't change for the person.** English still clings to *I am / he is* and *I eat / she eats*. Swedish has dropped even that: *jag äter, du äter, hon äter, de äter* — one form, always.

**No separate progressive tense.** *Jag äter* means both "I eat" **and** "I am eating". English makes you choose between *I eat* and *I am eating*; Swedish doesn't — the context tells you which one is meant. So never look for a Swedish word for the "am" in "I am eating".

**No masculine and feminine nouns.** Swedish does have two noun genders (*en* and *ett*), but they have nothing to do with male or female, and they don't change adjectives nearly as much as German does. That's for Unit 4, and it's much lighter than it sounds.

blocks.text: What needs attention from day one is the sound system, not the grammar. Two Swedish hissing sounds — **sh** and **hw** — are not quite like anything in English, and both turn up in very common words: *tjugo* (twenty), *kök* (kitchen), *sju* (seven), *station*. Go back to the pronunciation chapter as often as you need.

blocks.title: Lifesaver phrases
items: **Ursäkta, kan du prata långsammare?** — Excuse me, could you speak more slowly? (*ür-SHEK-tah, kahn dü PRAH-tah LONG-sahm-mah-reh*)
**Jag förstår inte.** — I don't understand. (*yah fö-SHTOHR IN-teh*)
**Vad betyder det?** — What does that mean? (*vah beh-TÜ-der deh*)
**Kan vi prata svenska? Jag övar.** — Can we speak Swedish? I'm practicing. Say this at the start of a conversation and Swedes won't switch to English.
